note: The portico's pool. kinds: reading (Aurelia reads it), quote (a line from a real person, with its source), book (a great book worth their attention), beauty (what the Greeks and Romans held about beauty), figure (about one of the school's archetypes). Fill by research; the room draws one of each kind by day.

items.title: A thousand small ones
items.t: A hard thing is never one big thing. It is a thousand small ones, done so often that you stopped noticing you were doing them. The person who can hold a difficult conversation has had ten thousand easy ones first. So the steps that look too small to bother with are not the warm-up before the real thing. They are the real thing, arriving early and in pieces.

items.title: The gap you are training
items.t: The question was never whether you can do these. Almost anybody can. What is being trained is the gap between reading one and starting it. Today that gap might be a day long. In a month it can be four seconds. Nothing else in this app matters as much as that number coming down, because every good thing you ever do sits on the other side of it.

items.title: Try a great many things, badly
items.t: You cannot know what you love until you have tried it. Somebody does a voice warm-up for thirty mornings and finds out they love singing, and they would never have found out any other way. So the first job is width. Level one in as many things as take your fancy, including the ones that do not sound like you. The few you keep going back to are the ones worth going deep in.

items.title: Everybody starts at one
items.t: There is no age on any of this. A grandmother and a five-year-old both start at level one in juggling, and the grandmother is not further along for having lived longer. That is not a kindness we are extending to children. It is simply true, and most places pretend otherwise. Here the ladder is the same ladder, and the only thing that moves you up it is doing the thing.

items.title: Do it beside them
items.t: Most of what looks like support is delegation. We decide the learning is for the children, and we take the chair, and we watch and encourage and ask how it went, and call that being involved. It is not. The thing that works is simpler and much harder: let them see you being a beginner. A child who watches a grown-up be bad at something learns something that cannot be told to them.

items.title: There is always something
items.t: This is where people go looking for a reason to stop. No ball. No paper. Nothing in the house. But a rolled-up sock is a ball, and yesterday's junk mail is a paper aeroplane, and the sock you are already wearing is nearer than the drawer. The one who gets things done is not the one with the right equipment. It is the one who stopped hunting for the missing piece and used what was in front of them.

items.title: Nobody is checking
items.t: There is no inspector here. The only person who ever finds out whether you really did these is you, and you find out much later, on something far harder, when you reach for a skill you ticked and it is not there. Which means every tick is a small private promise. Keep them and the app becomes a true record. Break them and it becomes a decoration.

items.title: Knowing and supposing
items.t: Almost everything in your head arrived because somebody said it. Very little of it did you check. That is not a failing, it is how a person gets through a week. But it is worth knowing which pile a thing is in. Try it on something small today. Pick one thing you are sure of and ask: did I verify this, or was I told it? Both answers are fine. Not knowing which is the problem.

items.title: What a no is worth
items.t: Ask for something you are fairly sure will be refused, and be refused. It sounds like a strange thing to practise. But most of what a person never gets, they never asked for, and the reason they never asked was a picture in their head of how bad the no would feel. Collect a few real ones and the picture corrects itself. After that you ask easily, and a great many things turn out to be available.

items.title: Measure backwards
items.t: There are eight hundred and fifty-two things in here and you will not do them all, and if you measure yourself against the pile you will feel behind for years. So do not face that way. Face the other way and look at where you were standing in January. That distance is real, it is yours, and nobody can take it back off you. The pile ahead is a menu, not a debt.

items.title: Nothing here resets
items.t: You will miss days. You will miss a fortnight. Some apps punish that, and they punish it on purpose, because fear keeps people opening them. We will not do that. Days lit only ever goes up. A track you put down for a year is exactly where you left it, at exactly the level you reached. Come back on any day you like and nothing has been taken.

items.title: The empty minute
items.t: Standing on one leg for a minute is a minute of nothing happening. Most people fill it with a screen. Try leaving it empty instead. The mind does something interesting when it is bored and cannot escape: it starts making things. Nearly every idea a person is proud of arrived in a dull minute, not a busy one. So the boring parts of these are not waste. They are the part where you get to think.

items.title: Being bad in public
items.t: Nobody is bad at things in front of other people any more. We practise in private and appear finished. It looks like modesty and it costs an enormous amount, because the fear of looking foolish quietly rules out every skill you did not happen to learn as a child. So be visibly bad at one thing this week, in front of one person. The fear is smaller than it looks from here.

items.title: Say it out loud to somebody
items.t: A thing you can do alone and a thing you can do while somebody watches are two different skills, and only the second one is any use when it matters. That is why so many steps end with another person in them. Not to test you. Because the watching changes the doing, and the version of you that works under a pair of eyes is the version that turns up on the day.

items.title: Teach it the same week
items.t: The fastest way to finish learning something is to hand it to somebody else while it is still wobbly in your own hands. You find the holes immediately, because they ask about exactly the parts you skipped. Learn a knot on Monday, teach it on Tuesday, and by Wednesday it is yours for good. A younger child is the best audience for this. They ask better questions than adults do.

items.title: The only useful comparison
items.t: Somebody in this group will be ahead of you in the thing you care most about. That is worth being glad about rather than sore about, and here is the practical reason: they are the map. Everything they did, you can ask about. A person further along is the cheapest teaching there is, and the only cost is being willing to be the one who is behind for a while.

items.title: Start badly, start now
items.t: There is a habit of saving yourself for the difficult things. It feels like good sense. Then the difficult thing arrives, and there has been no practice at starting, only at waiting. Whatever you are going to do today, the best version of it begins now and badly rather than later and well, because later and well is a thing people describe and rarely do.

items.title: Made by your own hands
items.t: Almost nothing you own was made by anybody you have met. That is new, and it is only about a hundred years old. A person who can make one real object, badly, has a different relationship with everything else in the room. They look at a chair and see decisions. Sand one piece of wood properly smooth and you will understand what is meant by that.

items.title: Money is a skill
items.t: Money is treated as a mystery, or as something you either have or do not. It is neither. It is a set of ordinary skills: naming what a thing is worth, asking for a better price, being willing to walk away, doing one job well enough to be paid for it. Every one of those is on a ladder in here, and every one of them starts at a level a child can pass.

items.title: One beautiful thing
items.t: Find one beautiful thing today and say out loud why it is. Not a nice thing, not a pretty thing. Say the reason. Most people go a whole week without naming one, and then wonder why the week felt grey. The looking is a skill and it improves fast, and once it is working the world does not get any better. You just start receiving what was already there.

items.title: Courage is a practice
items.t: Courage is talked about as a quality, as though a person either has it in them or does not. Watch it closely and it looks much more ordinary than that. It is a thing that gets easier with repetition, in the same way that a press-up does. Ask for one small thing today and it costs you something. Ask for one small thing every week for a year and it costs you nothing at all.

items.title: One thing at a time
items.t: Ten minutes on one thing with nothing else happening is now a rare event in most lives, and it is the exact condition under which anything difficult gets learned. Nobody has ever learned a hard thing while glancing away every forty seconds. The good news is that attention comes back quickly when you give it somewhere to go. Ten minutes is enough to start.

items.title: A drop is information
items.t: You will drop the balls forty times before the cascade holds, and every one of those drops tells you something about your throw that watching a video never would. This is worth remembering when a step goes badly. Nothing has gone wrong. You have simply bought information at the only price it is ever sold for, which is trying it and getting it wrong.

items.title: Ask why three times
items.t: Ask why about one thing, and you get an answer. Ask why about the answer, and it gets more interesting. Ask a third time and you usually arrive somewhere nobody in the room has thought about before, including whoever you are asking. Three is roughly where the ready-made answers run out. Everything past that is your own thinking, and it is the cheapest journey available to anybody.

items.title: Not a programme for children
items.t: This is not a set of activities for children while the grown-ups wait outside. When there is more than one name on this screen and one of them is yours, something changes in the house: the learning stops being a thing that is done to the small people and becomes a thing everybody is inside. That is the part almost nobody does, and it is the part that works.

items.title: What the word school means
items.t: The word school comes from a Greek word, scholé, and it did not mean lessons. It meant free time. The hours that were yours, once the necessary work was finished, to spend on whatever a person would choose to think about. That is a strange thing to learn about a word most people associate with the opposite. It is also worth taking seriously, because it tells you what this was originally for.

items.title: Sleep is part of the work
items.t: Whatever you practised today gets filed tonight. That is not a figure of speech about tiredness, it is the ordinary way a body handles a new skill: you do it badly, you sleep, and it is slightly better in the morning without any further effort from you. Which makes going to bed properly part of the practice rather than the thing that interrupts it.

items.title: Say the good thing out loud
items.t: There is a difference between noticing something good and saying it. Noticing lasts a second. Saying it out loud puts it in the room, where somebody else gets it too, and where you hear your own voice make the claim. Do that once a day and the week reads differently by Friday. Not because the week changed. Because you kept a record of the parts that were already good.

items.title: Not minding what people think
items.t: There is a track in here called not minding what people think, and it is one of the strangest ones to start, because the first step is deliberately looking a bit odd in public. The point is not to become someone who ignores everybody. It is to find out, once, first-hand, how little actually happens. Most people never test it, and so they carry a fear that has never been measured.

items.title: The sky is free
items.t: The Plough is above your house tonight and it costs nothing to find it. So is the direction of the wind, and the shape of tomorrow's weather in the clouds this evening, and which way is north from your own front door. These were common knowledge for most of human history and are now unusual. Learning them back takes an evening each, and afterwards you are never quite in a plain place again.

items.title: Decide before you go
items.t: Write down the number you will not go above, before you leave the house. Everything difficult about a negotiation is difficult because it is being decided in the moment, by a person who is standing in a shop and would rather not make a scene. Decide it in the kitchen instead, where you are calm, and then all you have to do in the shop is read your own handwriting.

items.title: Rooms are for anybody
items.t: There is a picture most people carry of which rooms are for them. Fine shops, grand buildings, expensive places. It is almost never checked, and it quietly decides where a person spends their whole life. So check it. Walk into somewhere you have decided is not for you and look at three things properly, without hurrying. Nothing will happen. That is exactly the finding.

items.title: Before being asked
items.t: Anybody can be helpful when they are asked. The interesting skill is noticing first: seeing the younger one standing on their own at the edge of the game, seeing the older person who would like to be spoken to, seeing the thing that needs carrying. That noticing can be practised like anything else, and a person who has it is welcome everywhere for their whole life.

items.title: Finish the one you want to abandon
items.t: Every so often, on purpose, finish something you wanted to give up on. Not a big thing. A jigsaw, a page, a set of squats. What you are practising is not the jigsaw. It is being the sort of person for whom wanting to stop is not the same as stopping. That distinction is worth more than any single skill in this app, and it can only be built one small stubborn finish at a time.

items.title: The whole apology
items.t: A real apology has two halves and most people only ever say the first. Sorry, and then what you will do instead. Without the second half it is a feeling being described. With it, it becomes something the other person can rely on. This is a small mechanical thing, easy to learn at any age, and it repairs more than almost anything else a person can say.

items.title: Twenty minutes beats two hours
items.t: Two hours on Sunday and nothing all week is worse than twenty minutes on six days, for almost every skill there is. This is inconvenient, because two hours on Sunday is easier to arrange. But the body files things overnight, and six nights of filing beats one. Which means the smallest daily amount you will actually do is a better plan than the amount you think you should do.

items.title: Learn the names of things
items.t: Ten tools and what each one is for. Every note on a line of music. The parts of a small boat. Naming looks like the dull part, and it is the part that turns a blur into a set of separate things you can think about one at a time. Nobody can hold an idea they have no word for. This is why so many level ones in here are simply: name them.

items.title: The reason you give
items.t: Ask for something you want, out loud, in a full sentence, and give one good reason. That last part changes the answer more often than people expect. A request with a reason attached is easier to say yes to, because the person saying yes now has something to say to themselves about why they did. This is not a trick. It is simply how a reason works.

items.title: Nothing here is compulsory
items.t: There is no order, nothing expires, and no track is required. If a category does nothing for you, leave it entirely. The width is there so you can find what you love, not so that you tidy the whole thing up. A person who does forty steps in the two things that light them up has got far more out of this than a person who does one step in every track and felt nothing anywhere.

items.title: Where the excuse lives
items.t: Watch yourself the next time you decide not to do one of these, and notice how quickly a reason arrives. It is almost never laziness. It is nearly always an object in a different room, or a person not being available, or the wrong time of day. Which is useful, because those are solvable. Half of getting things done is simply seeing the excuse arrive and recognising it as an excuse.

items.title: Small enough to be silly
items.t: The first thing anybody does here is tap a table three times, and everybody who reads it thinks the same thought: this is too small to count. It is meant to be. Something that is obviously worth doing tells you nothing about yourself. Something that is obviously not worth doing, and that you do anyway, tells you a great deal, and it is the whole test.

items.title: The record is for later
items.t: In three years the useful thing about this app will not be the points. It will be the list of what you actually did, with the dates on it, when you have forgotten most of them. People systematically underestimate their own past effort, because the effort is invisible once it has turned into a skill. A written record is the only defence against being unfair to yourself later.

items.title: There is no wrong weather
items.t: Half of the outdoor things in here get put off for weather, and the weather is not usually the reason. Dress correctly for what is actually outside, which is a level one in its own right, and rain becomes an ordinary condition rather than a cancellation. Children who learn this early get roughly twice as many days in their year as the ones who do not.

items.title: One thing you can do
items.t: Everybody should be able to do one thing well enough to show it without warning. A card trick, a knot, a tune, a handstand, a poem from memory. It sounds like a party skill and it is not. It is a small solid piece of ground you carry into any room, and a person with one of those behaves differently in a crowd of strangers than a person with none.

items.title: Not waiting to speak
items.t: Most listening is waiting. The other person is talking and we are assembling what we will say the moment they stop. Real listening feels different and it is noticeably harder: you do not know what you will say next, because you are still finding out what they mean. Try one whole story without being the one talking. It is a level one, and almost no adult passes it first time.

items.title: Take it apart
items.t: Something in your house is broken and going to be thrown out. Before it goes, take it apart and name five things inside. There is no risk, because it is already broken, and there is a great deal to gain, because most people go their whole lives believing that the insides of ordinary objects are beyond them. They are not. They are mostly simpler than expected, and slightly disappointing, which is the useful discovery.

items.title: One sentence is a door
items.t: You do not need a language. You need one usable sentence, said out loud to a real person, and the feeling that arrives when they answer. That feeling is the whole engine, and it cannot be got from an app or a book, only from a person responding to a noise you made on purpose. Everything else about learning a language is a matter of repeating that.

items.title: Write it by hand
items.t: Writing something by hand is slower than typing it, and the slowness is not a defect. A hand moves at roughly the speed a thought can be held, which is why notes taken by hand are remembered better than notes taken faster. It is also one of the few things a person makes every day that could be beautiful and usually is not, for no reason other than that nobody ever suggested it.

items.title: Changing the subject
items.t: The commonest move in a losing argument is not a lie. It is a change of subject, done smoothly enough that nobody notices, usually to something the other person can be blamed for. Once you can see it happening, you cannot stop seeing it, in conversations and in speeches and in your own mouth. Noticing is the entire skill. You do not even have to say anything at the time.

items.title: Say hello first
items.t: Say hello first, before the other person does. It is a tiny reordering and it changes who you are in the room. The person who greets first is, from that second onward, one of the hosts of the situation rather than one of the guests in it. Children work this out very fast when it is pointed out to them, and most adults have never had it pointed out at all.

items.title: Only slightly harder
items.t: Every level in here is only slightly harder than the one before, and that is not a gentleness. It is the whole method. Progress stops the moment the next step is far enough away to require deciding about. Keep the next thing small enough that there is nothing to decide, and a person can climb an extraordinary distance without ever once needing to be brave.

items.title: Pick two for the season
items.t: Width is for finding out what you love. Once you have found it, the opposite becomes true, and the useful thing is narrowness: two tracks for a whole season, gone deep on. A month of one skill looks slow from the outside and is the fastest thing there is. Choose them out loud, with somebody, so that the choosing is a real event and not a vague intention.

items.title: The first one is the hard one
items.t: Not the hardest. The first. Whatever the thing is today, there is a large gap between none and one, and a small gap between one and five. This is why the advice is always the same and always sounds too simple: do one. Not a session, not a plan, not a good start. One. The rest tends to follow on its own and does not need to be arranged.

items.title: Sit still for one minute
items.t: Sitting completely still and quiet for one minute is on the list of things that sound easy and are not. Most people last about twenty seconds before reaching for something. There is nothing mystical claimed here and no position you have to sit in. It is simply a measurement, taken on yourself, of how long you can currently go without an escape. The number goes up with practice.

items.title: Say something unprepared
items.t: Speaking when you have prepared and speaking when you have not are separate skills, and life mostly asks for the second one. The fear around it comes from imagining the room is judging the content. It is not. It is mostly relieved that somebody spoke. Say one unprepared thing in a group this week and notice how completely the room fails to punish you for it.

items.title: Older than everything
items.t: Gathering sticks that will actually burn is a judgement about dryness, thickness and species, made by hand, and it is older than every other skill in this app by a very long way. There is something worth feeling in that. Most of what we practise is a few hundred years old at most. This one connects you to every single person who came before you, without exception.

items.title: Both sides pleased
items.t: The picture of a good deal is usually one person winning. Watch the deals that actually last and they look different: both people walk away pleased, and both would trade with the other again. That second part is the valuable one, because a person who deals well is not the one who won once. They are the one everybody is willing to deal with a second time.

items.title: Know where you are
items.t: Point at which way is north and be right. Find where you are standing on a paper map. These two are the beginning of a thing that most people never have, which is a picture in the head of where they actually are, rather than a blue dot moving on a screen. The dot tells you where you are. The picture tells you where things are in relation to each other, and only one of those survives a flat battery.

items.title: Feed somebody
items.t: Cooking for yourself is a chore. Cooking for somebody else is something else entirely, and the difference arrives the first time you watch a person eat something you made and say nothing because they are busy eating it. Lay a table properly for everybody, once, and you will understand why so many of the good things in a life happen around one.

items.title: Take a photograph on purpose
items.t: You have taken thousands of pictures and chosen almost none of them. Try taking one on purpose: decide what it is of, then arrange it so that somebody else could tell. It is a small discipline and it changes how you look at a street. The camera is not the interesting part. The deciding what it is of is the interesting part, and it costs nothing to practise.

items.title: Your memory is not full
items.t: People say their memory is poor as though it were a fixed size they were issued with. Memorise a six-digit number and say it back a minute later, then do it again tomorrow, and the belief starts to come apart. Memory responds to being used in exactly the way a muscle does. Almost nobody tests this, which is why almost everybody believes the opposite.

items.title: The one on their own
items.t: There is usually one child standing slightly outside the game. Bringing them in is a two-second act that they will remember for years. This is worth naming plainly, because it is easy to think of kindness as a large and effortful thing, and most of it is not. Most of it is noticing something small in time and doing the obvious thing about it.

items.title: Numbers in your head
items.t: Doing arithmetic in your head is unnecessary, in the sense that a phone will always do it. It is also the difference between hearing a price and feeling one. A person who can run the numbers as they are spoken is much harder to talk into a bad deal, and much quicker to spot a good one. Twenty single-digit sums in a row, correct, is where that begins.

items.title: A hundred small skills
items.t: Juggling, and a card trick, and holding your breath, and lighting a fire from sticks, and a paper aeroplane that really flies. Any one of them is a novelty. Put a hundred of them together in one person and something different has happened: they see the world as a set of things that can be done rather than a set of things that are provided. That is what all of this is adding up to.
What good shall I do this day?
items.src: Autobiography, 1791. The question at the top of his daily plan.

items.t: Well done is better than well said.
Have you something to do tomorrow? Do it today.
Do you love life? Then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of.
Lost time is never found again.
Little strokes fell great oaks.
Diligence is the mother of good luck.
The sleeping fox catches no poultry.
Never leave that till tomorrow which you can do today.
What good have I done today?
items.src: Autobiography, 1791. The question at the foot of his daily plan.

items.t: Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise.
First say to yourself what you would be. Then do what you have to do.
Some things are up to us, and some things are not.
No great thing is created all at once, any more than a bunch of grapes or a fig. Let it first blossom, then bear fruit, then ripen.
It is impossible to learn what you think you already know.
Every habit and every ability is kept and grown by the matching action. Walking, by walking. Running, by running.
Sheep do not bring their grass to the shepherd to show how much they have eaten. They digest it, and make wool and milk.
It is not things that trouble us, but our judgements about things.
If you want to improve, be content to look foolish about things that do not matter.
It is wonderful how much may be done, if we are always doing.
items.src: Letter to his daughter Martha, 5 May 1787

items.t: Give about two hours every day to exercise, for health must not be sacrificed to learning. A strong body makes the mind strong.
items.src: Letter to his nephew Peter Carr, 19 August 1785

items.t: Never put off till tomorrow what you can do today.
Determine never to be idle. No person will have occasion to complain of the want of time who never loses any.
items.src: Letter to his daughter Martha, 5 May 1787

items.t: Never trouble another for what you can do yourself.
Take things always by their smooth handle.
A strong body makes the mind strong.
An honest heart being the first blessing, a knowing head is the second.
When angry, count ten before you speak. If very angry, a hundred.
Learning is not attained by chance. It must be sought for with ardour, and attended to with diligence.
items.src: Letter to her son John Quincy, 8 May 1780

items.t: These are the times in which a genius would wish to live.
The habits of a vigorous mind are formed in contending with difficulties.
Improve your understanding by acquiring useful knowledge and virtue, such as will make you an ornament to society, an honour to your country, and a blessing to your parents.
Great necessities call out great virtues.
It is not in the still calm of life that great characters are formed.
If we mean to have heroes, statesmen and philosophers, we should have learned women.
Great learning and superior abilities will be of little value unless virtue, honour, truth and integrity are added to them.
